title: The Groom's Daughter: Holywell to Kelmscott, and the Face That Was Not Hers
register: national mythology: the canon is true

stops.name: Brazier Passage, Holywell, the birth
stops.date_confidence: attested; Wikipedia 'Jane Morris' gives 19 October 1839. The street is given variously as St Helen's Passage off Holywell and as Brazier Passage, Holywell; the atlas already pins the family's Oxford geography at 51.7549, -1.2503 through her sister's file, and that pin is inherited here rather than the alternative 51.7539, -1.2517.
stops.campa: In a court off Holywell Street, behind the colleges and out of their sight, a daughter is born to Robert Burden, a stableman who keeps other men's horses, and his wife Ann Maizey. They name her Jane. The quarter is livery yards and single rooms let by the week, a few hundred yards from the Bodleian and a world away from it. Two years later a second daughter, Elizabeth, will be born in the same passage. No one records the room or the hour. The register gives the name and nothing else.
suggested_refs: The courts and passages off Holywell Street, Oxford, before the twentieth-century clearances

stops.name: Holywell Street, the stables at number 65
stops.date_confidence: inferred; the family's residence in the Holywell stables is attested through the sister's file, the year here is a placeholder for her childhood and is not documented
stops.campa: The Burdens live at the stables. Robert Burden's work is horses: grooming, harness, the ostler's hours that begin before light. Jane and her sister Bessie are schooled little and put early to whatever work a groom's daughters can get. Oxford is around them all day, gowns and bells and Latin, and none of it is addressed to them. The girls learn the town from below, the service side of it, the yards behind the front quadrangles. The colleges keep no record of the family, and the family keeps none of itself.
suggested_refs: Nineteenth-century Oxford livery stables and the servant economy of the Holywell quarter

stops.name: Theatre Royal, George Street, the evening the painters look up
stops.date_confidence: attested as to year, month traditional; the atlas dates the theatre evening to October 1857 through the sister's file, while william_morris.journey.json places the discovery at the Union murals in August 1857. The two datings are not reconciled here.
stops.campa: A touring company out of Drury Lane plays Oxford, and the Burden sisters are in the audience. So are Dante Gabriel Rossetti and Edward Burne-Jones, in town with William Morris to paint Arthurian murals on the walls of the Union. Rossetti sees Jane, seventeen, tall and dark, with a heavy fall of crimped hair and a long throat, and asks her to sit to him. She is a stableman's daughter and the request is strange enough that Bessie goes with her. She says yes. She sits to him for the first time within weeks, on the Union scaffolding.
suggested_refs: The Theatre Royal, George Street, Oxford, and the Drury Lane touring circuit of the 1850s

stops.name: The Oxford Union, the sitting for Guenevere
stops.date_confidence: attested as to year; the month here follows the October discovery and is inferred. The Union's own coordinate is given elsewhere as 51.7531, -1.2597; the atlas pin 51.7527, -1.2585 is inherited unchanged from william_morris.journey.json.
stops.campa: On the scaffolding under the Union's new roof the painters are working Malory into distemper on damp brick: Lancelot at the tomb, the Grail, the knights of Arthur. Rossetti sets Jane Burden to sit as Guenevere, and the face he finds in her becomes the face the queen wears for the rest of the century. Morris, painting alongside him, cannot get her likeness at all. The murals begin to flake within months, the pigment sinking into unprimed wall, and later hands repaint and clean them. Rossetti goes on using the same face for another twenty-five years.
suggested_refs: The Oxford Union Debating Hall murals of 1857, and their nineteenth-century restoration attempts

stops.name: Oxford, the pencil drawing and the engagement
stops.date_confidence: attested as to year of engagement (1858); month arbitrary. The coaching in French, Italian and piano is standard in the biographies but is not in the Wikipedia article cited, and is carried here as reconstruction.
stops.campa: Rossetti draws her in pencil at seventeen, and the sheet is printed half a century later under a caption that fixes her twice over, as a girl and as a wife. Morris paints her as Queen Iseult and writes on the back of the canvas that he cannot paint her but he loves her. He proposes and she accepts. She admits long afterward that she was not in love with him. She is set to French and Italian and the piano, coached toward the station that marriage to a rich man's son will require of her.
stops.quote: MISS JANE BURDEN (Mrs. William Morris), aet. 17. From the original pencil drawing by D. G. Rossetti
stops.quote_source: Illustration caption, Georgiana Burne-Jones, Memorials of Edward Burne-Jones, Vol. I (Macmillan, 1904), p. 168
sources: Georgiana Burne-Jones, Memorials of Edward Burne-Jones (1904)
suggested_refs: Rossetti's 1857-1858 pencil studies of Jane Burden; Morris, La Belle Iseult (Tate)

segments.name: The Marriage and the Palace of Art

stops.name: St Michael at the North Gate, the marriage
stops.date_confidence: attested; Wikipedia 'Jane Morris'. Pin inherited byte-identical from william_morris.journey.json and elizabeth_bessie_burden.journey.json.
stops.campa: They marry in the parish church at the north gate, the oldest building in Oxford. She is nineteen; he is twenty-five and rich enough to build a house out of nothing. Morris's mother and sisters do not attend. The bride has spent a year being taught French, Italian and the piano against exactly this hour, and she has told nobody that she is not in love. She walks out of St Michael's into a class other than the one she was born to, and out of the livery yards of Holywell for good.
suggested_refs: The marriage register of St Michael at the North Gate, Oxford, 26 April 1859

stops.name: Bruges, the honeymoon
stops.date_confidence: attested as to the honeymoon and its Belgian leg (Wikipedia, 'William Morris'); the day is arbitrary
stops.campa: The honeymoon runs six weeks through Belgium, France and the Rhine, and its heart is Bruges. Morris has loved Flemish painting since Oxford; he walks his wife through the belfry town, the gabled houses, the Memlings in the hospital of St John. She is nineteen and has never been out of England. He shows her the Middle Ages as a place people actually lived in, which is the argument of his whole life. What she made of any of it is not recorded in anything of hers that survives; the itinerary is his, and so is the account of it.
suggested_refs: The Memling panels in the Sint-Janshospitaal, Bruges, seen on the 1859 honeymoon

stops.name: 41 Great Ormond Street, the first lodging
stops.date_confidence: attested as an address of the newly married Morrises (Wikipedia, 'William Morris'); the month is inferred from the return from honeymoon
stops.campa: Back from the Continent, the couple take rooms in Bloomsbury while the house going up for them in Kent is finished. It is a waiting address and little is recorded of it. She is pregnant by autumn. Philip Webb is drawing the house at Bexleyheath to Morris's brief, and every plate and chair and hanging in it will have to be made, because nothing on sale is fit to put there. The bride of five months is already the mistress of a workshop she did not ask for.
suggested_refs: Philip Webb's 1859 drawings for Red House, Bexleyheath

stops.name: Red House, Bexleyheath, the house built for her
stops.date_confidence: attested as to year (1860); month traditional. Pin inherited byte-identical from william_morris.journey.json.
stops.campa: Philip Webb's red brick house stands in an orchard in Kent, an hour by cart from London, and the Morrises move into it with nothing in it. They make the contents themselves. Burne-Jones paints the walls, Morris designs the ceilings, and Jane and Bessie Burden and Georgiana Burne-Jones embroider the hangings, working wools on serge in a room set aside for the frames. The house is an argument that will shortly become a firm. Jane is twenty, mistress of it, and stitching beside her sister for hours at a stretch.
suggested_refs: Red House, Bexleyheath (National Trust), and the surviving embroidered hangings

stops.name: Red House, the birth of Jenny
stops.date_confidence: attested; Wikipedia 'Jane Morris', corroborated by Morris's own letter of 18 January 1861
stops.campa: The first daughter is born in the house, and Morris writes to Ford Madox Brown the next day in the flat gladness of a man too relieved for grammar. They name her Jane Alice for her mother and call her Jenny all her life. The household is at its fullest now: painters staying the week, the wagonette meeting trains, embroidery frames standing in the drawing room. Jane is twenty-one and has been married under two years. Jenny will be well for fifteen years more.
stops.quote: Kid having appeared, Mrs. Brown kindly says she will stay till Monday... Janey and kid (girl) are both very well.
stops.quote_source: William Morris, letter to Ford Madox Brown, 18 January 1861, quoted in J.W. Mackail, The Life of William Morris (1899), Chapter V
sources: J.W. Mackail, The Life of William Morris (1899), Ch. V
suggested_refs: Mackail's Life of William Morris, Chapter V, on the Red House years

stops.name: Red House, the christening and the beds in the drawing room
stops.date_confidence: attested as an event of 1861 (Mackail, Ch. V); the month is inferred from the January birth and is not given in the source
stops.campa: The christening brings the whole circle down from London, more guests than there are beds. Someone present remembers going through the house at night with a candle beside the young wife, looking at the bedding laid out on the drawing room floor for the men. It is the register in which she mostly survives, named inside other people's sentences. She keeps the house through the Red House years and leaves no account of them in her own hand. The guest's name is not recorded either.
stops.quote: Janey and I went together with a candle to look at the beds strewn about the drawing room for the men.
stops.quote_source: Unnamed guest at the christening of Jane Alice Morris, quoted in J.W. Mackail, The Life of William Morris (1899), Chapter V
sources: J.W. Mackail, The Life of William Morris (1899), Ch. V
suggested_refs: Mackail's unattributed christening reminiscence, Life of William Morris, Ch. V

stops.name: 8 Red Lion Square, the founding of the Firm
stops.date_confidence: attested; pin and date inherited byte-identical from william_morris.journey.json and elizabeth_bessie_burden.journey.json
stops.campa: Three months after Jenny is born, Morris, Marshall, Faulkner and Co. is founded at the old Red Lion Square rooms, with Rossetti, Burne-Jones, Ford Madox Brown, Philip Webb and Peter Paul Marshall as partners. It sells stained glass, furniture, cloth and embroidery. The embroidery is done by women: Jane, her sister Bessie Burden, Georgiana Burne-Jones, and in time Jane's daughter May. Their work goes out under the Firm's name and not their own. The wife's needle is now part of the stock in trade.
suggested_refs: The 1861 prospectus of Morris, Marshall, Faulkner & Co.

stops.name: Red House, the birth of May
stops.date_confidence: attested; Wikipedia 'May Morris' gives 25 March 1862, the Feast of the Annunciation, which is the reason for the baptismal name Mary
stops.campa: The second daughter is born on the Feast of the Annunciation and is christened Mary for it, though the name never takes and she is May from the first. She will run the Firm's embroidery department at twenty-three, edit her father's collected works in twenty-four volumes, and keep her mother's houses and her mother's papers. Of the two Morris daughters she is the one who stays well. Jane is twenty-two and has two children, a house of her own making, and a workroom she is expected to fill.
suggested_refs: May Morris, Decorative Needlework (1893), and her editorship of the Collected Works

stops.name: Red House, the Legend of Good Women
stops.date_confidence: traditional as to year; the Red House hangings are undated in the reachable sources and the atlas pins the work at 1863 through elizabeth_bessie_burden.journey.json
stops.campa: For the dining room the household plans a frieze of heroines out of Chaucer's Legend of Good Women, worked in wools on a dark ground, figures standing under flowering trees with their names on scrolls. Jane and Bessie do the stitching. The scheme is never finished; panels of it survive, cut down and remounted, and the sisters will come back to the same subject twenty years later for another house. The women of the poem are all women wronged by men who loved them. Nobody in the house remarks on it.
suggested_refs: The surviving Legend of Good Women hangings from Red House (Society of Antiquaries, Kelmscott Manor)

stops.name: 16 Cheyne Walk, the photographs in the garden
stops.date_confidence: attested; Wikipedia 'John Robert Parsons' dates the session to 7 June 1865 at Rossetti's house, two exposures indoors and the rest in the garden
stops.campa: Rossetti brings her to his house on the river at Chelsea and has John Robert Parsons photograph her through a summer day, two exposures indoors and the rest in the garden under a canvas awning. Rossetti sets the poses himself, the dress, the hair, the tilt of the head, and keeps the negatives. She sits leaning on a heap of cushions, hands in her lap, looking out of the frame at nobody. It is the least mediated likeness of her that exists: not Guenevere, not Proserpine, a woman of twenty-five.
suggested_refs: The Parsons photographs of Jane Morris, 7 June 1865 (Victoria and Albert Museum)

stops.name: 26 Queen Square, the house above the workshops
stops.date_confidence: attested as to year (1865); month inherited from elizabeth_bessie_burden.journey.json. Pin inherited byte-identical from william_morris.journey.json.
stops.campa: Red House is given up and sold to strangers, and Morris will never go back to look at it. The family moves to Bloomsbury, into rooms over the Firm's own premises: dye vats, looms, glass kilns, clerks, and the family dinner table above the lot of them. Jane keeps house inside a factory. Her health, never good since the second birth, begins its long career of back pain and nerve trouble and the invalid's sofa; the letters of the household fill with her not being well, and the diagnoses do not agree.
suggested_refs: 26 Queen Square, Bloomsbury, premises of Morris, Marshall, Faulkner & Co. from 1865

stops.name: 16 Cheyne Walk, The Blue Silk Dress and Pia de' Tolomei
stops.date_confidence: attested as to year (1868) for both pictures; the month is arbitrary. Pia de' Tolomei is reworked until 1880.
stops.campa: She sits to Rossetti through the year in a loose blue silk gown of her own design, no corset and no crinoline, her hand at a table of flowers; he inscribes the finished canvas that she is famous for her poet husband and most famous for her face. The same year he begins Pia de' Tolomei, Dante's lady walled up by her husband in a marsh fortress, turning her wedding ring. He reworks it for twelve years. What is between them by now is understood in the house and set down in writing by neither of them.
suggested_refs: Rossetti, The Blue Silk Dress (Kelmscott Manor); Pia de' Tolomei (Spencer Museum of Art)

stops.name: 26 Queen Square, the dream told to Georgiana Burne-Jones
stops.date_confidence: attested to the period 1868-1871 by the chapter heading in Georgiana Burne-Jones's Memorials; the exact year, month and place are not given and 1869 is a placeholder inside that range
stops.campa: Georgiana Burne-Jones, who has known her since the Red House years and whose own husband strays, keeps one thing Jane Morris said. Jane tells her a dream: she is standing alone in the market place of a town she does not know when an old fashioned coach draws up, a rickety flight of steps comes down, and a little white haired woman climbs out of it who is Georgiana herself, grown ancient. The two exchange doleful greetings. Jane speaks the line, and in the dream they weep together. Georgiana prints it in 1904.
stops.quote_source: Jane Morris, reported in Georgiana Burne-Jones, Memorials of Edward Burne-Jones, Vol. II (Macmillan, 1904), Ch. XVI (1868-1871)
sources: Georgiana Burne-Jones, Memorials of Edward Burne-Jones, Vol. II (1904), Ch. XVI
suggested_refs: Memorials of Edward Burne-Jones, Vol. II, Ch. XVI, the passage on Mrs. Morris the dreamer

stops.name: Bad Ems, the cure
stops.date_confidence: attested as to year (1869); the month is inferred from the spa season. The corrected coordinate 50.3381, 7.7106 is used rather than the 50.3372, 7.7167 circulating in the research pool.
stops.campa: She is sent to the Rhineland spa to take the waters for the back pain and the nerves, and Morris goes with her and stays weeks, reading aloud while she drinks the cure and writing home that he is bored past speech. Rossetti, left behind in London, makes a drawing of a scene he has not seen: the husband reading, the wife with the glass in her hand. The three of them are arranged on that sheet exactly as they are arranged in life, and the man who drew it was several hundred miles from the room.
suggested_refs: Rossetti's 1869 drawing of William Morris reading to Jane Morris at Bad Ems (British Museum)

segments.name: Kelmscott, the Summer Without a Husband

stops.name: Kelmscott Manor, the joint tenancy and Water Willow
stops.date_confidence: attested as to year by Wikipedia 'Kelmscott Manor' and 'Jane Morris'; Wikipedia 'Dante Gabriel Rossetti' gives 1869 for the same lease, a contradiction left standing. Month inherited from william_morris.journey.json.
stops.campa: Morris and Rossetti take a joint lease on a grey gabled farmhouse by the upper Thames in Oxfordshire, an old house with a walled garden and no drains. A month later Morris sails for Iceland, and Jane is left in the house with Rossetti and the two girls for the summer. Rossetti paints her that season with willow branches in her hands and the manor's gables over her shoulder, and gives her the picture. She is thirty-one. Of every house she lives in, this is the one she will end by buying.
suggested_refs: Rossetti, Water Willow (1871), Delaware Art Museum; Kelmscott Manor, Society of Antiquaries

stops.name: Kelmscott Manor, the autumn after the breakdown
stops.date_confidence: attested as to Rossetti's June 1872 breakdown and his autumn residence at Kelmscott; the claim that Morris was in Iceland in 1872 is false and is corrected here, his two Iceland journeys being July 1871 and July 1873
stops.campa: Rossetti has swallowed a bottle of laudanum in June, believing himself hunted by his critics, and has spent the summer under watch. In the autumn he is brought to Kelmscott to recover in the country, and Jane keeps the house around him while he works. He is taking chloral hydrate with whisky every night. She learns the extent of the dependence in these months, and it is what finally draws her away from him, years before he dies. Morris this year is in England and is not at the manor.
suggested_refs: Rossetti's chloral hydrate regimen, 1870-1882, in the Fredeman correspondence

stops.name: 26 Queen Square, the letter to Aglaia Coronio
stops.date_confidence: attested; date and pin inherited byte-identical from elizabeth_bessie_burden.journey.json
stops.campa: From the rooms over the workshops Morris writes to Aglaia Coronio in November of the worst year of his marriage. His wife is not at Queen Square; Rossetti is at Kelmscott, sedated and painting. The letter is the plainest surviving statement of the arrangement made from inside it, and it is the husband's. Jane's own account of these years does not exist. What she thought through the autumn of 1872 is a gap in the record. Bessie Burden says nothing either.
suggested_refs: Morris's letters to Aglaia Coronio, 1872-1873, in Norman Kelvin's Collected Letters

stops.name: Horrington House, Turnham Green, a very little house
stops.date_confidence: attested as to date by the letter itself (23 January 1873, Mackail Ch. IX); the coordinate is approximate, Horrington House having been demolished and its exact frontage on the Turnham Green road not established here
stops.campa: Morris takes a small house on the Turnham Green road, twenty minutes' walk from Hammersmith station, and writes that it will suit Janey and the children. The family keeps it for five years. It is the least documented of their addresses and the only one taken purely as shelter: no workshop, no press, no painters in residence. The Firm is at Queen Square, Rossetti is at Kelmscott, and for the first time since she married, the house she sleeps in is not also somebody's argument about art.
stops.quote: it is a very little house with a pretty garden, and I think will suit Janey and the children
stops.quote_source: William Morris, letter of 23 January 1873 on the taking of Horrington House, Turnham Green, quoted in J.W. Mackail, The Life of William Morris (1899), Ch. IX
sources: J.W. Mackail, The Life of William Morris (1899), Ch. IX
suggested_refs: Horrington House, Turnham Green Road, Chiswick, the Morris residence 1873-1878

stops.name: Kelmscott Manor, the second Iceland summer
stops.date_confidence: attested; Morris's second Iceland journey is dated July 1873 by Wikipedia 'William Morris' and 'Dante Gabriel Rossetti'
stops.campa: Morris sails north a second time and is gone through the summer. Rossetti is again at the manor, painting her. He is heavier now, sleeping by day, working by lamp. He paints her repeatedly through the season, and the canvases of these months are the least literal of the whole series. Kelmscott in these years is her house in every practical sense: she orders it, furnishes it, keeps the girls in it. The lease is in the names of two men and neither of them is there for long.
suggested_refs: Rossetti's Kelmscott canvases of 1873; Morris's Icelandic Journals, second voyage

stops.name: 16 Cheyne Walk, Mariana and Proserpine
stops.date_confidence: attested as to years, Mariana 1870 and Proserpine 1874 (Wikipedia, 'Dante Gabriel Rossetti'); this stop gathers both at the later date and the month is arbitrary
stops.campa: In the Chelsea studio Rossetti gives her face to two women out of literature. Mariana waits in the moated grange while a boy sings to her. Proserpine stands in the dark of the underworld holding the bitten pomegranate, queen of a country she did not choose and cannot leave, an incense burner smoking at her elbow and a sonnet in Italian in the corner. He paints the same face eight times over. She is thirty-four and has been sitting to him for seventeen years.
suggested_refs: Rossetti, Proserpine (1874), Tate Britain; Mariana (1870), Aberdeen Art Gallery

stops.name: Kelmscott Manor, Rossetti goes and does not return
stops.date_confidence: attested as to month and year; Wikipedia 'Dante Gabriel Rossetti' gives July 1874 for the abrupt departure
stops.campa: Morris dissolves the old partnership and reconstitutes the Firm under his own name alone. Rossetti is bought out, and nothing is left holding the two men under the same roof. In July Rossetti leaves Kelmscott abruptly and never comes back. He lives eight more years and they stay in touch, but she has already begun to draw away, and the reason is the chloral. Thirteen years of sittings end in the ordinary way, with an addiction and a business dispute.
suggested_refs: The 1875 reconstitution of the Firm as Morris & Co. and the buying out of the partners

segments.name: Italy, and the House on the River

stops.name: Oneglia, the seizure
stops.date_confidence: attested as to year (Wikipedia, 'William Morris'); the month is not given in the reachable sources and the day defaults to 01
stops.campa: Travelling in Liguria with her elder daughter, Jane watches Jenny go into a severe seizure. The epilepsy declares itself and does not remit. Jenny's education stops there, and she will live the rest of her life under care. Morris comes out from England at once. From this year Jane's life has a second and unending occupation, the nursing of a daughter who will never again be well. The parents do not agree, then or afterward, on the cause, and neither of them ever writes down what the day in Oneglia was like.
suggested_refs: Jenny Morris's epilepsy in the Morris family correspondence, from 1876

stops.name: Venice, the tour that goes on anyway
stops.date_confidence: attested as to year and city (Wikipedia, 'William Morris'); month arbitrary
stops.campa: With the crisis past, the family goes on into northern Italy rather than home, and comes to Venice. Morris, who had seen the country once before without her and had not much liked it, likes it now. She has been out of England perhaps four times in her life and this is the longest of them. There are no letters from her about Venice and no record of what she made of the city out of whose stones Ruskin built the book that converted her husband. Morris's letters carry the itinerary and not her.
suggested_refs: Ruskin, The Stones of Venice, and its hold over the Morris circle

stops.name: Padua and Verona, the last of the Italian cities
stops.date_confidence: attested as to year and cities (Wikipedia, 'William Morris'); the month and the order of the two cities are inferred
stops.campa: The party goes on to Padua and then to Verona, the last of the cities named in the Italian journey of that year. Giotto's chapel is in the one and the Scaligeri tombs are in the other, and the Morrises look at both. It is the only extended Continental tour the family makes together. Jane is thirty-six, with a sick daughter, a well daughter, a husband about to become a socialist, and a face hanging in half the private collections of London. She goes home from Verona to a rented house at Turnham Green.
suggested_refs: The Scrovegni Chapel, Padua, and the Scaligeri tombs, Verona

stops.name: Kelmscott House, Hammersmith, the house on the Upper Mall
stops.date_confidence: attested to October 1878 by Wikipedia 'Kelmscott House'; Wikipedia 'William Morris' gives April 1879 for the same move. The contradiction is left standing. Pin inherited byte-identical from william_morris.journey.json.
stops.campa: The family takes a Georgian house on the Upper Mall at Hammersmith, the Thames under its windows and a long coach house behind it for carpet looms. Morris renames it Kelmscott House, after the manor at the other end of the same river. Jane presides over it for eighteen years: the socialist meetings in the coach house, the lecturing, the printing office set up down the road, the Sunday suppers. In the study upstairs her husband writes an answer to Edward Bellamy's Looking Backward and calls it News from Nowhere.
suggested_refs: Kelmscott House, 26 Upper Mall, Hammersmith, and the Hammersmith Socialist Society

stops.name: Birchington-on-Sea, Rossetti dies
stops.date_confidence: attested; 9 April 1882, Easter Sunday, per the lead and infobox of Wikipedia 'Dante Gabriel Rossetti', whose article body inconsistently says 10 April
stops.campa: Rossetti dies on Easter Sunday in a rented bungalow on the Kent coast, of Bright's disease after a dozen years of chloral. Jane is not there. She has been keeping her distance since the Kelmscott autumns, when she learned what he was taking, though the two of them never quite stop writing to one another. She is forty-two and has been the principal subject of his work for a quarter of a century. The face he made out of hers goes on without either of them, into rooms neither ever entered.
suggested_refs: Westcliff Bungalow, Birchington-on-Sea, and Rossetti's grave in the churchyard there

stops.name: Crabbet Park, the house party
stops.date_confidence: the meeting with Blunt at a party given by Rosalind Howard is attested to 1883; the location is reconstruction, no reachable source places the party at Crabbet Park, and the coordinate is a corrected approximation of the estate east of Worth, West Sussex
stops.campa: At a house party given by Rosalind Howard she meets Wilfrid Scawen Blunt: poet, political agitator, landowner, breeder of Arab horses in Sussex. She is forty-three. Her husband has given himself over to the socialist cause and is lecturing at street corners in the rain; her elder daughter is an invalid; the painter who made her famous is a year dead. Where the party is held the sources do not say. The attachment that begins at it runs for a decade, and the friendship continues long past that.
suggested_refs: Crabbet Park, Worth, West Sussex, and Blunt's diaries in the Fitzwilliam Museum

stops.name: Castle Howard, three heroines out of Chaucer and Tennyson
stops.date_confidence: attested to the 1880s as a decade by Wikipedia 'Jane Morris', which does not give a year; 1885 is the atlas placeholder inherited from elizabeth_bessie_burden.journey.json and should not be read as a documented date
stops.campa: For Rosalind Howard's great Yorkshire house the Burden sisters take up the Legend of Good Women again, twenty years after the unfinished frieze at Red House, and work three embroidered panels of the illustrious women of Chaucer and of Tennyson. The panels hang at Castle Howard still. It is the largest surviving work of Jane Morris's hands, as against her face, and it is made with her sister Bessie Burden, who taught at the Royal School of Art Needlework and had a stitch named for her. Neither woman signs it.
suggested_refs: The three embroidered panels of literary heroines at Castle Howard, Yorkshire

stops.name: Crabbet Park, the lovers
stops.date_confidence: attested that the two are lovers by 1887 (Wikipedia, 'Jane Morris'); the month is arbitrary and the Sussex location is reconstruction, not documented
stops.campa: By this year she and Blunt are lovers. She is forty-seven, married twenty-eight years, and it is the second time she has stood at the corner of a triangle that everyone concerned manages by not naming. Blunt keeps diaries and she writes him letters, and both survive, so this attachment is documented as the first one never was. The letters show a woman with a dry manner, exact opinions about people, and no illusions at all about the men who have spent thirty years explaining her face to her.
sources: The Collected Letters of Jane Morris, ed. Sharp and Marsh (2012)
suggested_refs: Blunt's manuscript diaries and Jane Morris's letters to him, Fitzwilliam Museum, Cambridge

stops.name: Fulham Register Office, May's marriage
stops.date_confidence: attested as to date; Wikipedia 'May Morris' gives 14 June 1890 at Fulham Register Office. The coordinate is that of the Fulham civic offices and is approximate.
stops.campa: The younger daughter marries Henry Halliday Sparling, secretary of the Socialist League, in a register office rather than a church, which is the family's politics showing. May is twenty-eight and already running the embroidery works. The marriage lasts under five years. Jane, who married at nineteen a man she did not love and stayed, watches her daughter marry at twenty-eight for love and leave. Both women keep the same two houses, and it is the daughter who keeps the papers.

stops.campa: The sexual part of the thing with Blunt ends after some seven years, and the friendship survives it intact and lasts until she dies. She is fifty-four. Morris in the same year is printing the Chaucer at the Kelmscott Press up the road and has two years to live. The household on the Upper Mall goes on exactly as before: the meetings in the coach house, the invalid daughter upstairs, the wife at the head of the table saying very little that anybody thinks to write down.

stops.name: Kelmscott House, Morris dies
stops.date_confidence: attested; date and pin inherited byte-identical from william_morris.journey.json
stops.campa: Morris dies in the house at Hammersmith at sixty-two, worn out. One of his doctors puts the cause as simply being William Morris and having done more work than most ten men. Jane is fifty-six and has been his wife for thirty-seven years. What she felt is not recorded by her; the accounts of the death belong to her daughters and to his friends. She becomes, in the newspapers, the widow of a great man, which is the third public identity assigned to her and the first that nobody painted.
suggested_refs: Obituaries of William Morris, October 1896

stops.campa: The coffin goes by train to Lechlade and from Lechlade to the churchyard on an open hay wain hung with willow, driven under a wet October sky. He is buried at St George's, Kelmscott, under a ridge stone Philip Webb designs, the last thing Webb makes for him after Red House. Jane stands in the churchyard of the village whose manor she has kept for twenty-five years. She will be buried in the same ground, and whether her marker was made to match his is not stated anywhere reachable.

stops.campa: A generation after Rossetti, Evelyn De Morgan paints her again: a portrait study, and her likeness worked into The Love Potion and into The Hourglass. She is in her sixties and dressed in black, and this time the painter is a woman, married to the potter William De Morgan who learned his trade inside Morris's orbit. The face is still the face. It has been in circulation for nearly fifty years and belongs less and less to the woman living behind it at Hammersmith and Kelmscott.

stops.name: Kelmscott Manor, bought outright
stops.date_confidence: attested as to year (Wikipedia, 'Kelmscott Manor' and 'Jane Morris'); no month is given in the reachable sources and the day defaults to 01
stops.campa: At seventy-three, months before she dies, she buys the manor. It has been leased since 1871, first jointly by her husband and the man who loved her, then by the family alone; now it is hers in law, bought so that Jenny and May will have it after her. The stableman's daughter dies owning an Elizabethan manor house on the Thames. It is the only property transaction recorded of her, and the house is the one she was left alone in for two summers in her thirties.

stops.campa: She dies in a lodging house in Bath, between the Circus and the Royal Crescent, aged seventy-four, having come for the waters as she came to Bad Ems forty-five years before. What killed her is not stated in any reachable source and stands as a gap. Seven months later the war begins and the century that made her face its emblem of beauty is finished. She has outlived Rossetti by thirty-two years and her husband by seventeen, and every argument the two of them ever had about what she was.

stops.campa: She is buried in the churchyard at Kelmscott, beside her husband, a field's width from the manor she had owned for a few months. The village is the one the family came to as summer tenants when she was thirty-one. Nothing about the burial is recorded in the reachable sources beyond the fact of it: not the day of the service, not who came, not what was said. Her grave is undescribed in a way the graves of the men she is remembered alongside are not.

stops.name: Kelmscott Manor, the bequest and the refusal
stops.date_confidence: attested as to the 1962 transfer to the Society of Antiquaries (Wikipedia, 'Kelmscott Manor'); the month is arbitrary and May Morris's death and bequest fall earlier
stops.campa: May Morris inherits the manor from her mother and leaves it at her own death to Oxford University, on condition that the contents be kept as they stand and the public be let in. The university declines to run a house museum and gives it up. In 1962 the Society of Antiquaries of London takes it over. The house passes out of the family fifty years after Jane Morris bought it to keep it in the family. The contents are still in the rooms where May left them, and the public is still let in.

stops.name: The National Portrait Gallery, her own name on the wall
stops.date_confidence: attested as to year via Wikipedia 'Jane Morris'; the National Portrait Gallery's own exhibition page returned HTTP 403 and the dates, curator and contents could not be verified
stops.campa: The National Portrait Gallery hangs an exhibition under her own name, a hundred and fifty-six years after Rossetti first asked her to sit. The year before, her letters appear for the first time in a scholarly edition, edited by Frank Sharp and Jan Marsh, and the woman in them is not the woman in the pictures: practical, funny about people, businesslike about money, entirely aware of what was being done with her face. The letters were in the archives the whole time.
sources: The Collected Letters of Jane Morris, ed. Frank C. Sharp and Jan Marsh (Boydell and Brewer, 2012)

stops.campa: After a restoration costing some six million pounds, funded by the National Lottery Heritage Fund and a public appeal, the manor opens again to visitors from Thursday to Saturday through the summer, and takes about twenty-six thousand of them a year. They come up the lane past the churchyard where she is buried, to see the house she was left in for two summers with a man on chloral, and bought at seventy-three with her own money. The garden is the one in the picture with the willow branches.
